title: The Open Road
paragraphs: “Ratty,” said the Mole suddenly, one bright summer morning, “would you do me a favor, please? I have something to ask you.”

The Rat was sitting on the riverbank, singing a little song. He had just made it up himself, so he was far too wrapped up in it to give Mole, or anything else, proper attention. Since early morning he had been swimming in the river with his friends the ducks. Whenever the ducks suddenly stood on their heads, as ducks do, he would dive down and tickle their necks, just below where their chins would be if ducks had chins. Then they had to bob up to the surface in a hurry, sputtering and furious and shaking their feathers at him. It is impossible to say quite _all_ you feel when your head is underwater. In the end they begged him to go away, mind his own business and let them mind theirs. So the Rat left, sat down on the riverbank in the sunshine, and made up a song about them, which he called
“DUCKS’ DITTY.”

Along the quiet backwater,
By rushes tall and green,
Ducks go dabbling, dabbling,
Tails up, all unseen!
Ducks’ tails, drakes’ tails,
Yellow feet a-quiver,
Yellow bills below the surface,
Busy in the river!

Muddy green weeds below
Where the roach swim—
There we keep our pantry,
Cool and full and dim.

Each to his own delight!
_We_ love to be
Heads down, tails up,
Dabbling free!

High in the blue above
Swifts wheel and call—
_We_ are down dabbling,
Up tails all!
“I can’t say I think _all_ that much of that little song, Rat,” Mole remarked carefully. He was no poet himself and didn’t mind who knew it, and he was an honest sort of animal.

“Neither do the ducks,” the Rat answered cheerfully. “They say, ‘_Why_ can’t we do what we like, _when_ we like and _how_ we like, instead of other fellows sitting on banks watching us all the time, making remarks and poetry and things about us? What _nonsense_ it all is!’ That’s what the ducks say.”
“So it is, so it is,” said the Mole, very heartily.
“No, it isn’t!” cried the Rat, offended.
“Well, then, it isn’t, it isn’t,” said the Mole soothingly. “But what I wanted to ask was, would you take me to visit Mr. Toad? I’ve heard so much about him, and I’d love to meet him.”

“Why, of course,” said the good-natured Rat, leaping to his feet and putting poetry out of his head for the day. “Get the boat out, and we’ll paddle up there right now. There’s never a bad time to call on Toad. Early or late, he’s always the same fellow. Always cheerful, always glad to see you, always sorry when you leave!”
“He must be a very nice animal,” said Mole, climbing into the boat and taking the oars while the Rat made himself comfortable in the back.

“He’s truly the best of animals,” answered Rat. “So plain-hearted, so good-natured, and so loving. Maybe he isn’t very clever—we can’t all be geniuses—and he may well be both boastful and vain. But he has some fine qualities, has Toady.”
As they came around a bend in the river, a handsome, stately old house of weathered red brick came into view, its neat lawns stretching down to the water’s edge.

“That’s Toad Hall,” said the Rat. “See that creek on the left, where the sign says, ‘Private. No landing allowed’? It leads to his boathouse, and that’s where we’ll leave the boat. The stables are over there on the right. What you’re looking at now is the banqueting hall, which is very old. Toad is quite wealthy, you know, and this is honestly one of the nicest houses around here, though we never admit that to Toad.”

They glided up the creek, and the Mole pulled in his oars as they passed into the shadow of a large boathouse. Here they saw many handsome boats, hanging from the crossbeams or pulled up on a slipway, but none on the water; and the place felt unused and deserted.

The Rat looked around. “I see,” he said. “Boating is played out. He’s tired of it and done with it. I wonder what new craze he’s taken up now? Come along and let’s find him. We’ll hear all about it soon enough.”

They climbed out and strolled across the bright, flowery lawns looking for Toad. They soon found him resting in a wicker garden chair, with a preoccupied look on his face and a large map spread across his knees.

“Hooray!” he cried, jumping up when he saw them. “This is splendid!” He shook both their paws warmly, not waiting to be introduced to the Mole. “How _kind_ of you!” he went on, dancing around them. “I was just about to send a boat down the river for you, Ratty, with strict orders that you were to be brought up here at once, whatever you were doing. I need you badly—both of you. Now, what will you have? Come inside and have something! You don’t know how lucky it is that you turned up just now!”
“Let’s sit quietly for a bit, Toady!” said the Rat, dropping into an easy chair, while the Mole took another beside him and made a polite remark about Toad’s “delightful home.”
“The finest house on the whole river,” Toad bellowed. “Or anywhere else, for that matter,” he couldn’t resist adding.

At this the Rat gave Mole a nudge. Unluckily, Toad caught him at it, and his face turned bright red. For a moment there was an awkward silence. Then Toad burst out laughing. “All right, Ratty,” he said. “That’s just how I am, you know. And it isn’t such a bad house, is it? You like it yourself, you know you do. Now listen. Let’s be sensible. You’re exactly the animals I was hoping for. You’ve got to help me. It’s terribly important!”

“Something to do with your rowing, I’d guess,” said the Rat, looking perfectly innocent. “You’re coming along reasonably well, although you still throw up plenty of spray. Given loads of patience and heaps of coaching, you could——”

“Oh, pooh! Boating!” interrupted Toad, in great disgust. “A silly childish pastime. I gave that up _ages_ ago. A complete waste of time, that’s what it is. It honestly makes me sorry to see you fellows, who ought to know better, spending all your energy in such a pointless way. No, I’ve discovered the real thing, the only true occupation for a lifetime. I intend to devote the rest of mine to it, and I can only regret the wasted years behind me, squandered on trifles. Come with me, dear Ratty, and your agreeable friend too, if he’d be so good, just as far as the stable yard, and you’ll see what you’ll see!”

So he led the way to the stable yard, the Rat following with a deeply suspicious look; and there, pulled out of the coach house into the open, they saw a gypsy caravan, shining with newness, painted a canary yellow trimmed with green, and with red wheels.

“There you are!” cried Toad, planting his feet apart and puffing himself up. “Real life, right there, packed into that little cart! The open road, the dusty highway, the heath, the common, the hedgerows, the rolling downs! Camps, villages, towns, cities! Here today, up and away somewhere new tomorrow! Travel, change, interest, excitement! The whole world spread out in front of you, and a horizon that never stops changing! And mark my words, this is the finest cart of its kind ever built, with no exceptions whatever. Come inside and see how it’s all arranged. I planned every bit of it myself, I did!”
Mole was enormously interested and thrilled, and he hurried after Toad up the steps and into the caravan. The Rat merely snorted, jammed his hands deep in his pockets, and stayed right where he was.

It really was very compact and comfortable. There were little sleeping bunks, a small table that folded up against the wall, a cooking stove, lockers, bookshelves, a birdcage with a bird in it, and pots, pans, jugs and kettles of every size and kind.

“Everything’s here!” said Toad triumphantly, pulling open a locker. “You see—biscuits, potted lobster, sardines—everything you could possibly want. Soda water here—tobacco there—writing paper, bacon, jam, cards and dominoes—you’ll find,” he went on, as they came back down the steps, “you’ll find that absolutely nothing has been forgotten when we set off this afternoon.”
“Pardon me,” said the Rat slowly, chewing on a piece of straw, “but did I just hear you say something about ‘_we_,’ and ‘_set off_,’ and ‘_this afternoon?_’”

“Come now, Ratty, my dear, good old friend,” Toad begged, “please don’t get all stiff and sniffy about it, because you know perfectly well you’ve _got_ to come. I can’t possibly get along without you, so just call it settled and don’t argue, since that’s the one thing I can’t stand. You can’t really intend to spend your entire life stuck to that dull, musty old river of yours, living in a hole in the bank and only _boating?_ I’m here to show you the world! I’ll turn you into a proper _animal_, my boy!”

“I don’t care,” said the Rat stubbornly. “I’m not coming, and that’s final. I _am_ going to stay with my old river, _and_ live in a hole, _and_ go boating, just as I always have. What’s more, Mole is going to stay with me and do as I do, aren’t you, Mole?”

“Naturally I am,” Mole said loyally. “I’ll always side with you, Rat, and whatever you decide is how it has to be. Still, it does sound as if it might have been—oh, rather good fun, you know!” he added in a wistful voice. Poor Mole! The Life Adventurous was something so new and exciting to him, and this new side of it tempted him so much, and he had lost his heart at first glimpse to the canary-yellow cart and every one of its dear little fittings.

The Rat could see what was going through Mole’s mind, and he wavered. He hated letting people down, he was fond of Mole, and he would do nearly anything to please him. Toad was watching both of them closely.

“Come inside and have some lunch,” he said smoothly, “and we’ll talk it over. There’s no need to settle anything in a rush. Of course, _I_ don’t really care either way. All I want is to make you fellows happy. ‘Live for others!’ That’s my motto in life.”

During lunch—which was excellent, of course, as everything at Toad Hall always was—Toad simply let himself go. Ignoring the Rat, he proceeded to play on the inexperienced Mole as if he were a harp. Mole was naturally a talkative animal and always carried away by his imagination, and Toad painted the prospects of the trip, and the joys of the open life and the roadside, in such glowing colors that Mole could hardly stay in his chair for excitement. Somehow, it soon seemed to be taken for granted by all three that the trip was settled; and the Rat, though still not convinced in his own mind, let his good nature override his objections. He couldn’t bear to disappoint his two friends, who were already deep in schemes and expectations, planning each day’s separate activity for several weeks ahead.

Once everyone was ready, Toad, triumphant by now, marched his friends out to the paddock and put them to work catching the old gray horse. Nobody had asked the poor creature, and he was extremely put out: Toad had simply handed him the dustiest job of this whole dusty expedition. He frankly preferred the paddock, and he took a lot of catching. In the meantime Toad crammed the lockers even fuller of supplies, and hung nosebags, nets of onions, bundles of hay and baskets all along the underside of the cart. Finally the horse was caught and harnessed, and off they went, everybody talking at once. Each animal was either plodding along beside the cart or perched on the shaft, whichever suited his mood. The afternoon was golden. The dust their feet stirred up smelled rich and satisfying. Birds called and whistled cheerily to them from the thick orchards on both sides of the road. Friendly travelers passing by said “Good day,” or paused to say kind things about the handsome cart. And rabbits, sitting at their front doors in the hedgerows, threw up their front paws and cried, “Oh my! Oh my! Oh my!”

Late that evening, weary and happy and miles from home, they stopped on a lonely common far from any houses, let the horse loose to graze, and ate a plain supper on the grass beside the cart. Toad boasted at length about everything he meant to do in the days ahead, while the stars grew fuller and brighter around them, and a yellow moon, appearing suddenly and silently out of nowhere in particular, came to keep them company and listen to their talk. At last they went to their little bunks in the cart; and Toad, stretching out his legs, said drowsily, “Well, good night, you fellows! This is the real life for a gentleman! Talk about your old river!”
“I _don’t_ talk about my river,” said Rat, who was nothing if not patient. “You _know_ I don’t, Toad. But I _think_ about it,” he went on, sadly, dropping his voice, “I think about it—all the time!”

The Mole stretched an arm out from under his blanket, found the Rat’s paw in the dark, and squeezed it. “I’ll do whatever you want, Ratty,” he whispered. “Shall we slip away tomorrow morning, quite early—_very_ early—and go home to our dear old hole by the river?”

“No, no, we’ll see it through,” the Rat whispered back. “Thanks awfully, but I ought to stick by Toad until this trip is over. It wouldn’t be safe to leave him on his own. It won’t take long. His crazes never do. Good night!”
The end was indeed nearer than even the Rat suspected.

All that fresh air and excitement had left Toad sleeping like a log, and the next morning no amount of shaking would drag him out of bed. So Mole and Rat quietly and manfully got on with things themselves. Rat took charge of the horse, built the fire, scrubbed last night’s cups and plates and laid out everything for breakfast, while Mole set off on a long trudge to the nearest village for milk and eggs and the other supplies Toad had, naturally, forgotten to bring. By the time Toad finally strolled onto the scene, bright and merry, all the hard work had been done and the two of them were sitting about utterly worn out. He remarked what a pleasant, easy life they were all living now, compared with the cares and worries and wearisome chores of keeping house at home.

They had a pleasant ramble that day over grassy hills and along narrow side lanes, and camped as before on a common, only this time the two guests made sure that Toad did his fair share of the work. As a result, when it was time to start the next morning, Toad was by no means so enthusiastic about the simplicity of the primitive life, and in fact tried to climb back into his bunk, from which he was hauled out by force. Their way lay, as before, across country by narrow lanes, and it wasn’t until the afternoon that they came out onto the high road, their first high road; and there disaster, swift and unforeseen, leapt out at them—disaster that was momentous indeed for their expedition, but simply overwhelming in its effect on the later career of Toad.

They were strolling easily down the high road, with Mole at the horse’s head, chatting to him, because the horse had complained that he was being dreadfully left out and that nobody paid him the slightest attention. Toad and Water Rat walked behind the cart, talking together—or rather Toad was talking, while Rat said every so often, “Yes, exactly; and what did _you_ say to _him?_”—and thought all the while about something quite different. Then, far behind them, they heard a faint warning hum, like the drone of a distant bee. Glancing back, they saw a small cloud of dust with a dark, driving center, coming at them at an unbelievable speed, and out of the dust came a thin “Poop-poop!” that wailed like an animal in uneasy pain. They hardly noticed it and turned back to their conversation, when suddenly (or so it seemed) the peaceful scene was transformed, and in a blast of wind and a whirl of noise that sent them leaping for the nearest ditch, It was on them! The “Poop-poop” rang brassily in their ears. They caught one moment’s glimpse of an interior of glittering plate glass and rich leather, and the magnificent motor-car, huge, breathtaking, full of passion, with its driver tense and hugging his wheel, took possession of all the earth and air for a fraction of a second. It flung up a smothering cloud of dust that blinded them and wrapped them up completely, and then shrank to a speck in the far distance, turning back into a droning bee once more.

The old gray horse had been plodding along, dreaming of his quiet paddock, and in a raw, new situation like this he simply gave in to his natural feelings. Rearing, plunging and backing steadily, in spite of everything Mole did at his head and all the lively language Mole aimed at his better nature, he drove the cart backwards toward the deep ditch at the side of the road. It teetered for a moment—then there was a heartbreaking crash—and the canary-colored cart, their pride and joy, lay on its side in the ditch, a hopeless wreck.

Rat danced up and down in the road, simply beside himself with rage. “You villains!” he shouted, shaking both fists. “You scoundrels, you highwaymen, you—you—road-hogs!—I’ll have the law on you! I’ll report you! I’ll take you through every court in the land!” His homesickness had quite slipped away from him, and for the moment he was the captain of the canary-colored ship, run onto a sandbank by the reckless jostling of rival sailors. He was trying to remember all the fine, cutting things he used to say to the skippers of steam-launches when their wash, as they drove too near the bank, used to flood the parlor carpet at his home.

Toad sat straight down in the middle of the dusty road with his legs stretched out in front of him and stared fixedly after the vanishing motor-car. He was breathing in short gasps, his face wore a calm, satisfied look, and every now and then he faintly murmured “Poop-poop!”

Mole was busy trying to calm the horse, and after a while he managed it. Then he went to look at the cart lying on its side in the ditch. It was a sorry sight indeed. The panels and windows were smashed, the axles were hopelessly bent, one wheel was off, sardine tins were scattered all over the wide world, and the bird in the birdcage was sobbing pitifully and begging to be let out.
Rat came to help him, but even together they could not set the cart upright. “Hi! Toad!” they cried. “Come and lend a hand, can’t you!”

Toad never answered a word or moved from his seat in the road, so they went over to see what was the matter with him. They found him in a kind of trance, with a happy smile on his face and his eyes still fixed on the dusty trail left by their destroyer. Every now and then he could still be heard murmuring “Poop-poop!”
Rat grabbed him by the shoulder and shook him. “Well, Toad, are you going to give us a hand or not?” he demanded sternly.

“What a glorious, stirring sight!” murmured Toad, never offering to move. “The poetry of motion! The _real_ way to travel! The _only_ way to travel! Here today—in next week tomorrow! Villages skipped, towns and cities leapt over—always somebody else’s horizon! Oh, bliss! Oh, poop-poop! Oh my! Oh my!”
“O, _stop_ being an ass, Toad!” cried Mole in despair.

“And to think I never _knew!_” Toad went on in a dreamy drone. “All those wasted years behind me, and I never knew, never even _dreamed!_ But _now_—now that I know, now that I fully understand! O, what a flowery path lies spread before me from this day on! What clouds of dust shall rise behind me as I speed along my reckless way! What carts I shall fling carelessly into the ditch in the wake of my magnificent onrush! Horrid little carts—common carts—canary-colored carts!”
“What are we to do with him?” Mole asked Water Rat.

“Nothing at all,” Rat replied firmly. “There’s really nothing to be done. You see, I’ve known him for ages. He’s possessed now. He’s got a new craze, and it always takes him this way at first. He’ll go on like this for days, like an animal walking in a happy dream, quite useless for any practical purpose. Never mind him. Let’s go and see what can be done about the cart.”

A careful look showed them that even if they managed to set it upright by themselves, the cart would never travel again. The axles were in a hopeless state, and the missing wheel was smashed to pieces.

Rat looped the horse’s reins over its back and took it by the head, holding the birdcage, with its hysterical passenger, in his free hand. “Come on!” he told Mole grimly. “The nearest town is five or six miles off, and walking is all we can do. The sooner we get going, the better.”

“But what about Toad?” Mole asked anxiously as the two of them started out. “We can’t abandon him here, sitting in the middle of the road all by himself, in the state he’s in! It’s not safe. What if another Thing comes along?”
“O, _bother_ Toad,” said Rat savagely. “I’m done with him!”

They had not gone very far, however, when they heard a pattering of feet behind them, and Toad caught up with them and thrust a paw through the elbow of each, still breathing in short gasps and staring into empty space.

“Now listen, Toad!” Rat said sharply. “The minute we reach town, you’re going straight to the police station to ask whether they know anything about that motor-car and its owner, and to file a complaint about it. After that you need to find a blacksmith or a wheelwright and arrange to have the cart collected, repaired and set right again. That will take a while, but the wreck isn’t entirely hopeless. Meanwhile Mole and I will find an inn with comfortable rooms, and we’ll stay there until the cart is ready and your nerves have got over the shock.”

“Police station! Complaint!” Toad murmured dreamily. “Me, _complain_ about that beautiful, that heavenly vision I have been blessed with! _Mend_ the _cart!_ I’m finished with carts for all time. I never want to set eyes on that cart or hear it mentioned again. Oh, Ratty! You can’t imagine how much I owe you for agreeing to come along on this trip! I wouldn’t have set out without you, and then I might never have seen that—that swan, that sunbeam, that thunderbolt! I might never have heard that entrancing sound, or breathed in that bewitching smell! It’s all thanks to you, my dearest of friends!”

Rat turned his back on Toad in despair. “Do you see what we’re up against?” he asked Mole, talking over Toad’s head. “He’s completely hopeless. I give up. Once we’re in town we’ll head for the railway station, and with any luck we’ll find a train to take us back to the river bank tonight. And if you ever catch me going off on a pleasure trip with this maddening animal again!”—He snorted, and for the remainder of that weary trudge he spoke to nobody but Mole.

As soon as they reached the town, they marched to the station and parked Toad in the second-class waiting room, paying a porter twopence to watch him like a hawk. Next they left the horse in an inn’s stable and explained as best they could what was to be done about the cart and everything in it. Some time later a slow train set them down at a station not far from Toad Hall, and they led the spellbound, sleepwalking Toad to his front door, pushed him inside, and told his housekeeper to give him something to eat, get him out of his clothes and tuck him into bed. After that they fetched their boat from the boat-house and sculled home down the river, and very late indeed they sat down to supper in their own cozy riverside parlor, to Rat’s enormous joy and contentment.

The next evening Mole, who had got up late and spent the day taking it easy, was sitting on the bank with his fishing line when Rat, who had been out calling on friends and swapping gossip, wandered over to look for him. “Have you heard?” he said. “It’s all anybody is talking about, up and down the river bank. Toad took an early train up to Town this morning. And he has ordered a big, very expensive motor-car.”
